title: Lipid-transfer proteins in biosynthetic pathways.
text_summary: 本文综述脂质转运蛋白（LTP）在非囊泡脂质运输和脂质生物合成网络中的作用，比较OSBP/ORP、START、Sec14、PITP、GLTP等家族的结构域、定位和底物。CERT、FAPP2、OSBP、PITP等蛋白把内质网、高尔基体和质膜之间的神经酰胺、糖鞘脂、固醇及磷脂酰肌醇代谢连接起来，并参与膜运输和细胞信号。作者将LTP视为脂质代谢通路的整合器和分支开关，同时指出其体内脂质转运活性仍难直接测量。

Lipid-transfer proteins in biosynthetic pathways
Giovanni D’Angelo, Mariella Vicinanza and Maria Antonietta De Matteis
Compartmentalization is a deﬁning feature of eukaryotic cells
that allows the spatial segregation of different functions, such
as protein and lipid synthesis, and ensures their ﬁdelity and
efﬁciency. This imposes the need for an intense ﬂux of
metabolic intermediates between segregated enzymatic
activities, as seen for the sequential transport of
neosynthesized proteins through the segments of the secretory
pathway during their post-translational modiﬁcation. For lipid
synthesis, the identiﬁcation of proteins that transfer lipids
between membranes has revealed an additional mechanism for
this intercompartment exchange. The intense interest elicited
by the lipid-transfer proteins over the last few years has led to
the deﬁnition of their central role in key processes, such as lipid
metabolism, membrane trafﬁcking, and signaling.

Introduction
In addition to being structural components of cell mem-
branes, lipids have key roles in processes as diverse as
vesicular trafﬁcking, signal transduction, and transcrip-
tional regulation, with the easily predictable consequence
being that they are important determinants of cell fate
and differentiation, and of organism development. Such a
variegated range of functions is mirrored by the wide
repertoire of lipid species; indeed, a signiﬁcant portion of
the eukaryotic genome ( /C245%) is dedicated to lipid
metabolism, and this results in the generation of thou-
sands of different products [ 1].
The main center for lipid synthesis is the endoplasmic
reticulum (ER) [ 2], though important lipid biosynthetic
reactions occur at the Golgi complex [ 3,4], at the plasma
membrane [5,6
/C15], in the endosomal/lysosomal system [ 7],
and at the mitochondria [ 8]. The compartmentalized
metabolism of lipids and their distribution from their site
of synthesis to other cell districts rely on intense lipid
ﬂuxes. These can occur via three main mechanisms:
incorporation into membrane-sealed transport carriers
(i.e. vesicular trafﬁcking), diffusion along membrane
bilayers and between closely apposed membranes, and
active transfer by speciﬁc lipid-transfer proteins (LTPs).
The ﬁrst mechanism accounts for the vast majority of the
lipid ﬂux through the endomembrane system. However,
substantial lipid exchange has been demonstrated be-
tween endomembranes and compartments not belonging
to the endomembrane system, such as between the ER
and the mitochondria, and has been suggested to occur
between compartments of the endomembrane system
that are not directly connected through vesicular trafﬁck-
ing, such as between the ER and the plasma membrane,
the ER and the trans-Golgi, the ER and endosomes, and
the ER and lipid droplets [ 9,10,11
/C15/C15,12–14,15/C15]. Given
the hydrophobic nature of lipids and their low propensity
to spontaneously leave a membrane, this nonvesicular
lipid transport cannot be mediated by their free diffusion
in water-based environments. Rather, there needs to be
either a close proximity between the two lipid-exchan-
ging membranes and/or the involvement of the LTPs in
such nonvesicular lipid transport [ 16].
The LTPs are operationally deﬁned as proteins that
facilitate/accelerate lipid exchange between membranes
in vitro. They are characterized by the presence of a lipid-
binding pocket that shows different speciﬁcities both
toward the lipid headgroup and the backbone. Many
LTPs have been identiﬁed in eukaryotes, and on the
basis of their lipid-binding domains they can be subdi-
vided into the SEC14, PITP, START, GLTP, SCP-2
(nonspeciﬁc LTPs), and OSBP/ORP families. Although
named after their abilities to transfer lipids in vitro ,a
recurrent conundrum in the ﬁeld is whether the physio-
logical roles of the LTPs are actually related to their in
vitro transfer activities at all, or are instead because of the
more general ability of these proteins to bind speciﬁc
lipids, and thus to act as lipid sensors or lipid chaperones
that ‘present’ the bound lipid to metabolic enzymes.
Exemplars of ‘genuine’ in vivo LTPs [ 17,18] have been
recently identiﬁed in the ceramide-transfer protein
CERT [11
/C15/C15] and the glucosylceramide (GlcCer)-transfer
protein FAPP2 [ 19/C15/C15]. This has been possible thanks to
the involvement of these LTPs in lipid biosynthetic
pathways and thus to the availability of measurable and
direct read-outs of their in vivo lipid-transfer activities in
the end-lipid products of these pathways, such as sphin-
gomyelin (SM) and the glycosphingolipids (GSLs),
respectively [ 11
/C15/C15,19/C15/C15].

Roles in lipid metabolism are, however, only one aspect of
the many important functions that have been reported for
the LTPs, such as those in membrane trafﬁcking and cell
signaling. Here the question is to what extent are these
diverse functions inter-dependent, or whether at least
some LTPs belong to the expanding class of multifunc-
tional proteins? In the following, we will bring together
the recent advances in our understanding of the functions
of some of the LTPs, while focusing on those with
important roles in membrane trafﬁcking and cell sig-
naling, such as sec14/PITP, Oshs/ORPs, CERT, and
GLTP/FAPP2 ( Figure 1 ).
Domain organization and structure of the
LTPs
The LTPs exist both as ‘monodomain’ proteins that
essentially consist of their lipid-binding domain, and as
multidomain proteins ( Figure 1 ). Many of the LTPs, or
their lipid-binding domains, have been crystallized, and
for at least one member for each family the crystal
structure has been solved in association with the lipid
ligand ( Figure 1 ).
The PITPs are proteins that can transfer phosphatidyl-
choline (PtdCho) and phosphatidylinositol (PtdIns) be-
tween membranes in vitro [20]. The mammalian genome
contain ﬁve genes encoding PITPs (PITP a, PITP b,
RdgBa1/Nir2, RdgB a2/Nir3, and RdgB b), while the
yeast genome encodes six related proteins where the
prototype is Sec14p, which shares the same lipid-transfer
activity, but has neither sequence nor structure homology
with the mammalian PITPs [ 21]( Figure 1 ). The crystal
structures of PITP a and PITP b complexed with their
ligands have been solved [ 22–24]. The PITP domain
itself consists of a lipid-binding cavity that can be closed
by a ‘lid’, with the headgroup of the bound lipid buried
deep inside the cavity and the acyl chains pointing toward
the lid. The interaction with membranes triggers a con-
formational change that induces the opening of the lid
region, with the possibility of lipid cargo exchange [ 21].
The RdgB members of the PITP family (also referred to
as the Class II PITPs) differ from the Class I PITPs
(PITPa and PITP b) in that they are multidomain
proteins. In addition to the N-terminal PITP domain,
RdgBa contains a FFAT (two phenylalanines in an acidic
tract) motif that targets proteins to the ER via an inter-
action with VAP (vesicle-associated membrane-protein-
associated protein), six hydrophobic stretches, and a
PYK2-binding domain [ 25]( Figure 1 ). The PITP
domains of the RdgB proteins from different species
transfer PtdIns in vitro [26,27], while at least the Droso-
phila DrdgBa can transfer PtdCho as well [ 28].
The crystal structure of the major yeast PITP, Sec14p,
has been solved in its apo form [ 29], and molecular
dynamics simulation analysis has suggested the lipid-
transfer of Sec14p might be regulated by the opening
of a very conserved ‘gate helix’ that shows a high motility
and is controlled by two ﬂanking ‘hinges’ [ 30]. This
prediction has been conﬁrmed by the recently solved
structure of the closest homolog of Sec14, Sfh1 [ 31
/C15/C15]i n
its lipid-bound form (with PtdCho, PtdEtn, and PtdIns).
The most striking difference between the holo-Sfh1 and
the apo-Sec14 structure is in fact repositioning of the
conserved ‘gating helix’ that leaves open the lipid-bind-
ing pocket in the apo form and closes it in the lipid-loaded
form. A further intriguing feature of this LTP is that while
bound PtdCho is buried in the hydrophobic pocket, the
PtdIns headgroup-binding site lies near the Sec14 sur-
face. This would create a kinetic mismatch during the
PtdCho/PtdIns exchange on Sec14, with the entering
PtdIns being delayed in a partially incorporated state
that would be highly susceptible to PI-kinase activity
[31
/C15/C15].
CERT has been characterized as a cytosolic factor that
can drive the nonvesicular transport of ceramide from the
ER to the Golgi complex [ 11/C15/C15]. CERT consists of an N-
terminal pleckstrin homology (PH) domain, a coiled-coil
and a FFAT motif, and a C-terminal steroidogenic acute
regulatory protein-related lipid-transfer (START)
domain ( Figure 1 ). The START domain of CERT is
sufﬁcient to promote ceramide transfer in vitro [11
/C15/C15], and
has been crystallized in the apo and ligand-bound forms
[32/C15]. Interestingly, the size and shape of the hydrophobic
walls of the lipid-binding cavity dictates the limit of the
length of the aliphatic chains of ceramide, which accounts
for the observed transfer speciﬁcity toward C14–C20
ceramides, rather than longer amide acyl-chain ceramides
[33].
OSBP has a similar domain organization to CERT, in that
it consists of an N-terminal PH domain, a region contain-
ing a FFAT motif, and a C-terminal lipid-transfer domain
that in the case of OSBP is an oxysterol/cholesterol-
binding/transfer domain (OxB) [ 34]( Figure 1 ). OSBP
has been shown to bind sterols via its OxB domain,
though there is at present no speciﬁc evidence of an in
vivo transfer activity [35,36
/C15/C15]. OSBP is the prototype of a

larger family of OSBP-related protein (ORP) including 12
members in humans [ 34]( Figure 1 ).
The crystal structure and lipid-transfer activity of a yeast
OSBP ortholog, Osh4/Kes1p, have been characterized
[15/C15,37/C15]. The structure analysis of Osh4/Kes1p in its
apo and ligand-bound forms has suggested that the access
of the sterol molecule to the hydrophobic tunnel may be
regulated by a ﬂexible N-terminal lid region that is kept
closed in the sterol-bound form [ 37
/C15]. Moreover, the apo-
Osh4/Kes1p exposes a potential phospholipid-binding
region that might be involved in membrane docking
and lipid exchange.
A different family of LTPs is represented by the glyco-
lipid-transfer proteins GLTP and the GLTP-homology-
domain-containing protein FAPP2 [38]. For both of these,
transfer activities toward glycosylated derivatives of cer-
amide have been demonstrated in vitro [19
/C15/C15,39/C15/C15]. The
structure of GLTP has been solved in both the apo and
ligand-bound form, and the transfer speciﬁcity has been
explained by the ability of GLTP to organize hydrogen
bond networks with the sugar amide headgroup of gly-
colipids [ 39
/C15/C15]. Interestingly, GLTP accommodates its
ligand in a ‘moulded-to-ﬁt’ hydrophobic tunnel and thus
it could desorb glycolipids from membranes undergoing a
ligand-assisted conformational switch that produces the
lipid-binding pocket. FAPP2 is a larger protein that shares
its domain organization with CERT and OSBP. Indeed,
FAPP2 contains an N-terminal PH domain and a C-
terminus GLTP-homology domain ( Figure 1 ). Although
the crystal structure of FAPP2 remains to be determined,
all of the residues that have been shown to be important
for the lipid-transfer activity of GLTP are conserved in
FAPP2, and homology modeling of FAPP2 on the GLTP
structure produces signiﬁcant and reliable overlap [ 19
/C15/C15].
LTPs in lipid metabolism
A number of the LTPs have been directly implicated in
lipid metabolism where they have been suggested to
provide the enzymes with their speciﬁc substrates.
Sec14/PITP. A clear correlation exists between Sec14p
and both PtdIns and PtdCho metabolism in yeast cells
[40]. SEC14 loss-of-function produces an increase in
PtdCho levels in Golgi membranes [ 41], as well as a
signiﬁcant decrease in PtdIns(4) P levels [ 42]. SEC14 is
an essential gene in yeast, and genetic analyses have
identiﬁed seven nonessential yeast genes where their
ablation restores growth in SEC14-deleted strains [ 43–
46]. Five of these seven Sec14-bypass mutations occur in
genes encoding enzymes involved in the CDP–choline
pathway of PtdCho synthesis, one occurs in the SAC1
gene that encodes a phophoinositide phosphatase, and
the last involves the gene encoding the above-mentioned
LTP Osh4/Kes1p. Overexpression of the Golgi-localized
PtdIns 4-kinase (PI4K) Pik1p is also able to alleviate the
SEC14 loss-of-function phenotypes, highlighting again a
link with phosphoinositide metabolism [ 42].
Phosphoinositide metabolism begins in the ER with the
synthesis of PtdIns, which is the substrate of an array of
PIKs that can lead to the production of seven different
phosphorylated derivatives. The PIKs have distinct intra-
cellular distributions, which results in localized pro-
duction of each of these phosphoinositides. In yeast,
PtdIns(4)P is mainly produced by two PI4Ks: the
Golgi-localized Pik1p, and the plasma-membrane-loca-
lized Stt4p [47]. Sec14p is localized on Golgi membranes,
from where it can possibly supply Pik1p with its substrate
PtdIns after having extracted it from the ER membranes.
The role of Sec14p in PtdCho metabolism is less clear.
PtdCho is mainly produced in the ER via PtdEth meth-
ylation, or in the Golgi complex via the CDP–choline
pathway. Sec14-PtdCho negatively regulates PtdCho
synthesis by inhibiting the activity of the rate-limiting
enzyme in the CDP–choline pathway, choline cytidylyl-
transferase [ 30]. The relevance of the PtdCho transfer
activity of Sec14p in this regulation remains to be deﬁned.
The Class I PITPs have also been shown to support
PtdIns phosphorylation [21]. Moreover, they are involved
in the maintenance of the PtdIns(4,5) P
2 pool that is
consumed by phospholipase C (PLC) during agonist-
triggered signal transduction [ 48], and they can interact
with the EGF receptor, PI4K and PLC- g upon EGF
stimulation [ 48]. PITP a and PITP b differ in their intra-
cellular distributions, with the former being in the cytosol
and nucleus, and the latter being associated with the
Golgi complex [ 48]( Figure 2 ). This distribution is con-
sistent with a function for PITP a in plasma membrane
phosphoinositide metabolism [ 49,50], and for PITP b in
PtdIns(4)P production at the Golgi complex.
Among the Class II PITPs, RdgB a1/Nir2 has been
suggested to control diacylglycerol (DAG) levels at the
Golgi complex by acting on the CDP–choline pathway in
a way analogous to Sec14p in yeast [ 51].
CERT was identiﬁed in a genetic screening as the factor
responsible for reduced SM levels in a CHO cell line
[11
/C15/C15]. It has been shown that, thanks to its ability to bind
both Golgi membranes and the ER via its PH domain and
FFAT domain, respectively, CERT operates the shut-
tling of ceramide from the ER to the Golgi-localized
SMS1 [ 52], thus promoting SM synthesis ( Figure 2 )
[11
/C15/C15].
Osh/OSBP. The Osh4/Kes1p loss of function has been
shown to impair the esteriﬁcation of exogenously added
cholesterol in yeast [ 15/C15]. Since cholesterol esteriﬁcation
occurs in the ER, it has been suggested that Osh4/Kes1p
provides the plasma-membrane-to-ER transport of sterols.

OSBP1 has also been linked to cholesterol esteriﬁcation
and synthesis in mammalian cells [53], while whether these
effects depend on a lipid-transfer activity remains to be
understood.
GLTP/FAPP2. GLTP has been shown to contribute to the
nonvesicular transport of GlcCer from the Golgi complex
to the plasma membrane [ 54
/C15]( Figure 2 ). GSL metab-
olism is marginally affected by the loss of GLTP [ 55],
while it is severely impaired after the loss of the other
GlcCer-transfer protein, FAPP2 [ 19/C15/C15,54/C15]. Indeed,
FAPP2 has been demonstrated to promote the intra-Golgi
nonvesicular transport of GlcCer that is required for the
synthesis of complex GSLs [ 19
/C15/C15]. The ability of FAPP2
to transfer GlcCer to the ER has also been reported by
Halter et al. [54
/C15]( Figure 2 ).
LTPs as switches in the branching of lipid
metabolic pathways: the case of the COF
family proteins
CERT, OSBP and FAPP2 have been proposed to belong
to the same protein family, the COF family, as they share
a common domain organization and contain a highly
similar PH domain at their N-terminus [ 56]( Figure 1 ).
CERT and FAPP2 act directly on two different branches
of sphingolipid biosynthesis (i.e. SM and complex GSL
synthesis) [ 11
/C15/C15,19/C15/C15] while OSBP has been proposed to
act as a sterol sensor [57/C15]. The evolutionary occurrence of
these three proteins is of particular interest, since it
appears to be directly related to the evolution and branch-
ing of the sphingolipid biosynthetic pathway ( Figure 4 ),
thus suggesting a role for these LTPs in governing and
controlling the increasing specialization and complexity
of lipid metabolic pathways and lipid species in higher
eukaryotes.
OSBP orthologs are found among ciliates, yeasts (asco-
myces) and plants (angiosperms). CERT and OSBP
orthologs coexist in nematodes and insects, while FAPP2,
CERT and OSBP orthologs coexist in cnidarians, echi-
noderms, ﬁsh, birds, and mammals ( Figure 3). Given this
differential occurrence, an evolutionary model of the
COF family of LTPs can be proposed. OSBP appears
to be the most ancient member as it is present among
virtually all of the eukaryotes, CERT is most probably a
metazoan acquisition, and FAPP2 is apparently restricted
to deuterostomes (echinoderms and vertebrates)
(Figure 3 ). This order of occurrence of these LTPs
through evolution parallels the increase in complexity
of the sphingolipid synthetic pathway, which passes from
the three phytoceramide derivatives in yeast, to about a
hundred ceramide derivatives in mammals ( Figure 3 ).
This is mainly achieved through different levels and
orders of branching in the pathway that gives rise to
the variegated repertoire of GSLs in mammals.
The mechanisms underlying this branching are only
partly clear, and the existence of preassembled distinct
multienzymatic complexes has been invoked as one of
the ways that a common precursor can be channeled
toward different end products [ 58,59]. The LTPs might
represent key elements in this process, by acting as
controllers at the branching points of the sphingolipid
synthetic pathway. With their ability to transfer their lipid
substrate independently of vesicular trafﬁcking, the
LTPs can mediate a bypass of the ‘bulk ﬂow’ progression
of lipid precursors and their processive glycosylation
along the obligated sequential stations of the secretory
system. In this way, the LTPs can determine the meta-
bolic fate of their substrate lipid. Thus, in metazoans,
CERT would be instrumental in controlling the balance
between the two metabolic fates of ceramide, which is
converted into GlcCer if it is transported through vesicu-
lar trafﬁcking to the cis-Golgi (where GlcCer synthase
resides), or is converted into SM if it is transferred directly
by CERT through nonvesicular transport to the late Golgi
compartments (where SMS1 resides) [ 11
/C15/C15,60]( Figure 2).
Similar considerations can be applied in vertebrates to
GlcCer and FAPP2, which can deliver GlcCer to the later
Golgi compartments, thus potentially bypassing the inter-
mediate glycosylation steps that occur in the earlier Golgi
compartments ( Figure 2 ). The production of different
GSL series can therefore be ﬁne-tuned in this way.
LTPs as integrators of lipid metabolic
pathways
Cellular homeostasis is achieved through pervasive con-
nectivity between the different metabolic pathways, and
the LTPs are important elements in ensuring such con-
nectivity between lipid metabolic pathways ( Figure 4 ).

PtdIns(4)P is a binding partner of Osh4/Kes1p on Golgi
membranes [ 37
/C15]. Thus the transfer of sterols from or to

PtdIns(4)P production that is promoted by Sec14p [ 42].
On the contrary, Osh4/Kes1p has been proposed to act as
a buffering system for PtdIns(4) P at the Golgi complex
and to have an inhibitory effect on Pik1p [ 61/C15], which
would thus switch off the production of PtdIns(4) P at the
Golgi complex. In addition, as noted above, the anchoring
of Osh4/Kes1p to membrane phospholipids depends on
its sterol-binding state. This would mean that Osh4/
Kes1p controls PtdIns(4) P production/availability as a
function of the cell sterol content, thus linking sterol
and phosphoinositide metabolism in yeast ( Figure 4 ).
A further example comes from the PITPs and the COF
family of LTPs that are emerging as crucial integrators of
phosphoinositide, sphingolipid, and sterol metabolism.
The PITPs have been proposed to sustain PtdIns(4) P
production at the Golgi complex [ 21], with the con-
sequence that they may be involved in the recruitment
of the COF (CERT, OSBP, and FAPP2) family members
to the Golgi complex via their PtdIns(4) P-binding PH
domain [ 56]. The recruitment of CERT and FAPP2, in
turn, promotes the synthesis of SM and GSLs, respect-
ively [ 11
/C15/C15,19/C15/C15,62], thus creating a link between phos-
phoinositide and sphingolipid metabolism ( Figure 4). By
fostering SM synthesis, CERT also stimulates the pro-
duction of DAG: DAG is required for the recruitment to
the Golgi complex of PKD, which phosphorylates and
activates PI4KIII b, a signiﬁcant source for PtdIns(4) P at
the Golgi complex. PKD also phosphorylates and inacti-
vates CERT [ 63
/C15]( Figure 4 ).
Finally, functional connections also exist between the
individual members of the COF family, and in particular
between CERT and OSBP [ 57/C15]: it has been shown that
CERT-promoted SM synthesis can be stimulated by the
oxysterols in an OSBP-dependent manner [ 57/C15]
(Figure 4 ). The precise molecular mechanisms under-
lying this regulation are not understood, though a role that
has been suggested for oxysterol-bound OSBP indicates
an enhancement of CERT binding to ER and Golgi
membranes (and thus of ceramide transfer) [ 57
/C15].
LTPs in membrane trafﬁcking
The ﬁrst demonstration that LTPs have pivotal roles in
membrane trafﬁcking came from the seminal studies of
Bankaitis et al. [64]o n Sec14 in yeast. The Sec14 loss of
function produces remarkable defects in membrane traf-
ﬁcking from the Golgi complex to the plasma membrane
with minor impact on other membrane trafﬁcking steps
[65]. It was then shown that defects in both PtdIns and
PtdCho metabolism are responsible for the secretory phe-
notype in Sec14-null strains, as this could be reverted by
mutations in enzymes belonging to these two pathways
(see above). Thus, the requirement forSec14 in membrane
trafﬁcking has been attributed to its involvement in con-
trolling the production of DAG and of PtdIns(4) P at the
trans-side of the Golgi complex, two lipids that have key
roles in the formation of plasma-membrane-destined trans-
port carriers at the Golgi complex [40]. As for the PITPs in
mammals, both PITPa and b were originally found to be
required for reconstituting regulated secretion and for
vesicle formation in permeabilized cells [ 66,67]. More
recently, a role for RdgB a1/Nir2 in Golgi function has
been reported and attributed to its ability to modulate
DAG levels at thetrans-Golgi network (TGN) via negative
control of the CDP–choline pathway [ 51].
With the Osh/OSBP group, an indication that they are
involved in membrane trafﬁcking came from the obser-
vation that the ablation of Osh4/kes1 corrected the
secretory phenotype in Sec14-null cells [ 45]. A further
and independent demonstration that Osh4/Kes1 is
involved in membrane trafﬁcking comes from a gen-
ome-wide visual screening that showed that Osh4/Kes1
(together with several genes involved in ergosterol
metabolism) is required in the intracellular trafﬁcking
of a detergent-resistant-membrane-associated protein
[68]. The ability of Osh4/Kes1 to impact on PtdIns(4) P
metabolism at the Golgi complex (see above) underlies its
activity in the secretory pathway; however, an additional
and recently described feature of Osh4/Kes1p might also
be relevant here: Osh4p/Kes1p has an ALPS (ArfGAP1
lipid packing sensor) motif in its N-terminal 29 amino
acids, a lipid-packing sensor motif that promotes the
association of proteins to highly curved membranes [ 69].
A role for Oshs in endocytosis has been reported in yeast
[70]. This is consistent with the twofold possibilities that

The direct involvement of Oshs in an endocytic complex
would not be surprising considering that an OSBP-related
protein ORP1L is a Rab7 effector on late endosomes,
where it forms a heterotrimeric complex with RILP and
Rab7 [71
/C15]. This complex mediates the recruitment of the
microtubule motor adaptor protein dynactin, and facili-
tates its interaction with the general dynein membrane
receptor bIII spectrin, thus having a central role in
endosome motility [ 71
/C15].
FAPP2 was originally identiﬁed as a protein involved in
TGN-to-plasma-membrane transport, and in particular in
the formation of transport carriers at the TGN [ 72]. It was
then shown to be required for the transport of apical cargo
in polarized epithelial cells, where it is also involved in
the formation of the primary cilium [73,74]. The nature of
FAPP2 as a GlcCer-transfer protein was then demon-
strated both in vitro and in vivo [19
/C15/C15,54/C15]. Interestingly,
the two activities of FAPP2, in TGN-to-plasma mem-
brane trafﬁcking and as a GlcCer-transfer protein, appear
to be related, as a single point mutant of FAPP2 that
cannot transfer GlcCer is also not able to rescue the
secretory defect in FAPP2-knockdown cells [ 19
/C15/C15]. What
remains to be deﬁned is to what extent the trafﬁcking
defect in FAPP2 depleted cells is a consequence of
impaired GSL synthesis, in line with the reported role
of GSLs in Golgi secretory/sorting functions [ 75–77], and
to what extent this is because of a role for GlcCer transfer
at the site of transport carrier formation at the TGN. This
is an intriguing possibility considering that the transfer of
lipids to the cytosolic leaﬂet of membranes, such as with
FAPP2, would be a way to induce local membrane
asymmetry and thus to promote the budding of transport
carriers [ 78].
The role of CERT in membrane trafﬁcking has been
shown recently with the demonstration that a CERT
knockdown inhibits the release of a soluble secretory
reporter protein. In this case, the impaired secretory
activity has been viewed as a direct consequence of
the impaired SM synthesis and DAG production at the
Golgi complex (see above) [ 63
/C15]. Indeed, DAG is crucial
for the Golgi secretory function. It is a strongly conical
lipid that can per se induce membrane bending, fusion,
and ﬁssion [ 78], and it can act as a scaffold/activator
component for the PKD-controlled ﬁssioning machinery
at the TGN [ 79].
LTPs in cell signaling
The two main examples of the LTPs being involved in
cell signaling are those of Rdg/PITP and OSBP.
Mutations in Drosophila DrdgBa produce light-induced
retinal degeneration [ 80]. In the ﬂy eye, the detection of
light is associated with a classical signaling pathway
involving G-protein-coupled PtdIns(4,5) P
2 hydrolysis
through PLC [81]. In DrdgBa mutants, the PtdIns(4,5)P2
levels in photoreceptor cells after stimulation are sub-
stantially lower than in control cells, suggesting a defect
in the replenishing of the PtdIns(4,5) P2 pool [ 82] and
pointing toward a role for DrdgB a in transferring PtdIns
to the plasma membrane of photoreceptor cells for local
conversion to PtdIns(4,5) P2. A similar role has been
hypothesized for PITPs, that, as noted above, have a role
in the maintenance of the PtdIns(4,5) P
2 pool that is used
by phospholipase C (PLC) in response to receptor-acti-
vation [48]. In addition PITP have been shown to interact
with plasma membrane receptors [ 48,50].
OSBP has also been attributed a role in cell signaling
since it has been shown to be involved in cholesterol-
regulated dephosphorylation of extracellular-signal-
regulated kinase (ERK) [ 36/C15/C15]. Depletion of membrane
cholesterol increases the levels of pERK because of
inhibition of the activity of a cholesterol-regulated phos-
phatase with dual speciﬁc activity for pERK. The dual
speciﬁcity is because of the coexistence in a hetero-
oligomer of two phosphatases, one belonging to the
PTPPBS family of tyrosine phosphatases, and the other
being the serine/threonine phosphatase PP2A [36
/C15/C15]. The
two enzymes each depend on the activity of the other to
coordinately remove phosphate from both the threonine
and the tyrosine residues of pERK. Depletion of mem-
brane cholesterol results in the dissociation of PP2A from
the PTPPBS member, and hence a loss of this dual
speciﬁcity pERK phosphatase activity. It has been shown
that cholesterol acts here through OSBP, as the oligomer
is held together through interactions between cholesterol
and OSBP [ 36
/C15/C15]. How is this signaling role of OSBP,
which is presumably at the plasma membrane, combined
with its role and localization at the Golgi complex? The
model that has been proposed is that cholesterol binding
induces a conformational change in OSBP that masks the
Golgi-targeting PH domain, and that primes OSBP for its
interaction with the phosphatases; upon oxysterol binding
or cholesterol dissociation, OSBP would release the phos-
phatases and expose the PH domain, to be recruited again
to the Golgi complex [ 83]. This would be an intriguing
scenario, where the function and site of action of a LTP
would depend on the bound lipid species, and it thus
represents an interesting paradigm to be explored not
only for OSBP, but also for the other LTPs.
Concluding remarks
The LTPs have emerged as key components of lipid
metabolic pathways, membrane trafﬁcking and cell sig-
naling. The importance of these various roles of LTPs for
the cells and for the organism is testiﬁed by the severe
consequences for human health that can be induced by
Lipid-transfer proteins in biosynthetic pathways D’Angelo, Vicinanza and De Matteis 367
www.sciencedirect.com Current Opinion in Cell Biology 2008, 20:360–370

 

their genetic defects [ 84]. In spite of the enormous
advances in the deﬁnition of the structures of many LTPs
and in our understanding of their cellular roles, the same
question has still been dominating the ﬁeld from the start:
are the roles of the LTPs in cells, and more importantly,
in the organism, actually related to their abilities to
transfer lipids in vitro? The continuing lack of a response
is, however, due to methodological limitations and to the
impossibility of measuring lipid transfer in vivo . Over-
coming this barrier is the challenge for the coming years.
